The amount of time allotted to individual speakers shall be determined based on the total number of persons requesting to speak during this item. Procedures for Removing Items from the Consent Calendar
:
Members of the public who request to remove an item from the consent calendar must first discuss the item with a staff member by phone or a back-and-forth email discussion, and state the name of the staff member when requesting removal of the item from the consent calendar
(by 2 p.m. the day of the meeting)
.  The procedures for discussion do not apply to items sponsored by the mayor or councilmembers.
Any member of the City Council who would like to remove an item from the consent calendar must notify the appropriate staff person and the City Clerk’s Office prior to the meeting. Although members of the City Council are encouraged to ask questions and share concerns with staff ahead of the meeting, they are not required to do so.
The Clerk’s Office must be informed of any requests to remove items from the Consent Calendar. Items removed from the Consent Calendar shall be placed at the end of the agenda for consideration.
CONDUCT AT MEETINGS:
Richmond City Council meetings are limited public forums during which the City strives to provide an open, safe atmosphere and promote robust public debate. Members of the public, however, must comply with state law, as well as the City’s laws and procedures and may not actually disrupt the orderly conduct of these meetings. The public, for example, may not shout or use amplifying devices, must submit comment cards and speak during their allotted time, may not create a physical disturbance, may not speak on matters unrelated to issues within the jurisdiction of the City Council or the agenda item at hand, and may not cause immediate threats to public safety.

Accessibility for Individuals with Disabilities:
Upon request, the City will provide for written agenda materials in appropriate alternative formats, or disability-related modification or accommodation, including auxiliary aids or services and sign language interpreters, to enable individuals with disabilities to participate in and provide comments at/related to public meetings. Please submit a request, including your name, phone number and/or email address, and a description of the modification, accommodation, auxiliary aid, service or alternative format requested at least two days before the meeting.  Requests should be emailed to
[email protected]
or submitted by phone at 510-620-6513, ext. 9, or 510-620-6509.  Requests made by mail to City Clerk’s Office, City Council meeting, 450 Civic Center Plaza, Richmond, CA 94804 must be received at least two days before the meeting. Requests will be granted whenever possible and resolved in favor of accessibility.
Unless otherwise noted in an agenda description, all actions taken by the Council include a determination that CEQA does not apply (i.e., the action is not a project and therefore exempt from CEQA).

Devin W.
I'm in support of continued use of ALPR technology and switching to Axon from Flock.

This isn't theoretical. Just last month in El Cerrito, after that city removed its own license plate cameras, police said the loss of that data slowed the investigation into the murder of 21-year-old Jakai Couch. It was fixed and ALPR cameras in Richmond that ultimately helped identify the suspects' vehicle and led to two arrests so far.

Here in Richmond, fixed and ALPR cameras also helped identify the suspect in the fatal hit-and-run that killed 81-year-old Rafael Gutierrez Delgado last month.

These aren't abstract benefits. These cases have suspects in custody and their families have timely answers they might not have gotten otherwise, if ever.

As with any surveillance technology, I support ALPR with appropriate guardrails including 30-day retention limits, regular audits, clear policies on who can query the data and why, and meaningful oversight and accountability when something goes wrong.

I also prefer Richmond owning the cameras vs. leasing them, and having the data stored with evidence.com.

Richmond has actually led the Bay Area on this front. As far as I'm aware, we're the only city in the region operating a closed ALPR system, meaning our data isn't shared out to other agencies by default or choice in California (and nationally). That's the best model, so don't abandon it.
Edith Alderette
I've watched this topic for years, and until recently, I was agnostic. I see both the pros and cons of the ALPR systems. Recent events, particularly the recent El Cerrito murder and the hit-and-run homicide on 23rd St. where cameras were key to apprehending the suspects, have changed my mind. ALPRs have saved numerous people, apprehending in minutes suspects in murders and child abductions that otherwise may have taken hours, days, or weeks; time that would allow the criminals to do even more harm. The key is these systems need to be used RESPONSIBLY, and I believe RPD will do just that. I venture to guess that opponents so dead set against ALPRs would be all for them had their child was abducted, assaulted, or murdered and police are unable to do anything because they have no leads. The alternative is a residential dragnet, which is even more invasive. How many more major crimes in Richmond must go unsolved before we can accept that this is the best solution available to us? And it's not as if these systems are permanent; if and when better technology exists, we can remove them. These are the tools we have now, and we need them. Recently, in our neighborhood, two thieves attacked children in their own driveway.

Everything is imperfect, including the ALPRS system. But that doesn’t mean that the criminals take priority over the taxpayers.

Devin W.
I'm in support of continued use of ALPR technology and switching to Axon from Flock.

This isn't theoretical. Just last month in El Cerrito, after that city removed its own license plate cameras, police said the loss of that data slowed the investigation into the murder of 21-year-old Jakai Couch. It was fixed and ALPR cameras in Richmond that ultimately helped identify the suspects' vehicle and led to two arrests so far.

Here in Richmond, fixed and ALPR cameras also helped identify the suspect in the fatal hit-and-run that killed 81-year-old Rafael Gutierrez Delgado last month.

These aren't abstract benefits. These cases have suspects in custody and their families have timely answers they might not have gotten otherwise, if ever.

As with any surveillance technology, I support ALPR with appropriate guardrails including 30-day retention limits, regular audits, clear policies on who can query the data and why, and meaningful oversight and accountability when something goes wrong.

I also prefer Richmond owning the cameras vs. leasing them, and having the data stored with evidence.com.

Richmond has actually led the Bay Area on this front. As far as I'm aware, we're the only city in the region operating a closed ALPR system, meaning our data isn't shared out to other agencies by default or choice in California (and nationally). That's the best model, so don't abandon it.
Edith Alderette
I've watched this topic for years, and until recently, I was agnostic. I see both the pros and cons of the ALPR systems. Recent events, particularly the recent El Cerrito murder and the hit-and-run homicide on 23rd St. where cameras were key to apprehending the suspects, have changed my mind. ALPRs have saved numerous people, apprehending in minutes suspects in murders and child abductions that otherwise may have taken hours, days, or weeks; time that would allow the criminals to do even more harm. The key is these systems need to be used RESPONSIBLY, and I believe RPD will do just that. agenda_briefs.summary: Richmond City Council will receive an informational presentation from the Bay Area Air District on the preliminary Health Risk Assessment (HRA) of the Chevron Richmond Refinery, released August 25, 2026 under Rule 11-18. agenda_briefs.title: Council to consider directing city manager to present detailed financial report
agenda_briefs.summary: Council will consider directing the city manager to present a detailed financial report at the October 20, 2026 Council meeting. The report would cover the City's finances from fiscal year 2023-24 through 2026-27, including revenue, expenses, surplus or deficit, allocated surplus, and reserves. It would also include information on funds received from the Chevron settlement, such as allocations, balance, interest earned, and total settlement balance as of September 30, 2026. The report would present financial data by prior-year budget projection, Council-approved budget, midyear budget revision, budget at close, actuals at close, and audited financial statements. The city manager would also be directed to engage a qualified municipal advisor to independently review the financial information for accuracy and consistency.
